title: Connections and pools
summary: Why a database connection is expensive, sizing pools with Little's law, the arithmetic behind "sorry, too many clients already", PgBouncer transaction pooling and what it breaks, and the views seniors query first.

steps.title: Connections are not free
body: PostgreSQL runs **one server process per connection**. Each costs memory (a few MB, more with large
`work_mem` sorts), and thousands of them compete for CPU and locks even when mostly idle. That is why
`max_connections` is a hard limit (the default is 100) and why every app keeps a **pool** of open
connections instead of opening one per request.
```text
60 app instances × pool of 20  =  1,200 connections wanted
PostgreSQL  max_connections = 800   →  400 refused:
FATAL:  sorry, too many clients already
The trap is that the total grows with the **number of instances**, not with traffic. Autoscaling the app
tier during a spike multiplies connections at exactly the moment the database is busiest.

steps.explain: Pools fill lazily, so this often appears minutes after a scale-out, when traffic grows and the late pools try to open their connections.

steps.title: Size the pool with Little's law
body: Little's law says the number of things in a system equals arrival rate × time each spends there. For a
pool: **connections in use = queries per second × seconds per query**.
```text
one instance: 400 queries/s × 5 ms = 2 connections busy on average
add headroom for bursts (×1.5)    → a pool of 3 is plenty
A bigger pool does **not** make a busy database faster. Once the database CPUs are saturated, more
concurrent queries only add contention and context switches, so each query gets slower. A well-known
starting point for the database side (from the HikariCP pool-sizing notes) is about
`cores × 2 + effective disks` active connections. Requests beyond that should **wait in the app's pool**,
where waiting is cheap and visible, not inside the database.
In .NET with Npgsql the pool is on by default; set its size in the connection string:
`Host=db.example.com;Database=shop;Maximum Pool Size=10;Timeout=5`.

prompt: **Symptom first.** At 12:03 the app autoscaled from 20 to 60 instances for a sale. From 12:05 about a third of
requests fail. The database CPU is only 45 %. App logs:
code: Npgsql.PostgresException (0x80004005): 53300: sorry, too many clients already
options: The pools of the new instances exceed `max_connections`: put PgBouncer (or the cloud's proxy) in front in transaction mode, or shrink each pool so instances × pool fits
The database is overloaded: buy a bigger instance
steps.explain: SQLSTATE 53300 (`too_many_connections`) with a calm CPU is a connection-count problem, not a load problem. Raising `max_connections` far up costs memory per process and moves the collapse to when those connections all get busy. Retries add more connection attempts.

steps.title: PgBouncer: many clients, few server connections
body: PgBouncer sits between the apps and PostgreSQL, accepts thousands of client connections and shares a
small number of real server connections between them. `pool_mode` decides when a server connection is
given back:
| `pool_mode` | Server connection is returned | Fits |
| `session` | when the client disconnects | anything, but saves little |
| `transaction` | after each transaction | most web apps; the usual choice |
| `statement` | after each statement | autocommit-only workloads; multi-statement transactions are refused |
In **transaction** mode, consecutive transactions of one client may run on different server connections,
so anything tied to a **session** breaks: `SET` without `LOCAL`, session-level advisory locks,
`LISTEN`, temporary tables kept across transactions. Protocol-level prepared statements used to break
too; PgBouncer 1.21 and later can track them when `max_prepared_statements` is set above zero.

steps.prompt: Behind PgBouncer in `pool_mode = transaction`, does this work?
steps.explain: Transaction-scoped things travel with the transaction, so they are safe. Session-scoped things stay on a server connection that the next transaction may not get. Run listeners and session-heavy jobs on a direct connection.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: what is the database doing?
steps.body: When the database is slow or refusing connections, these answer "who is connected, what are they running, and what is expensive?"

toolkit.what: The hard connection limit. Compare it with instances × pool size across every service that connects.
One row per connection: who, from where, what state, what query, waiting on what.
flags: `active`, `idle`, `idle in transaction` (holding locks and a connection)
`Lock`, `IO`, `LWLock`... why an active query is not running
set it in the connection string to tell services apart
toolkit.example: SELECT application_name, state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
toolkit.when: connection errors, or a pile-up of waiting queries

toolkit.what: Totals per normalised query since the last reset: calls, total and mean time, rows, buffers. The top of `total_exec_time` is where the database spends its life.
flags: ms spent in this query in total
pages read from outside shared buffers
toolkit.example: SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS mean_ms, left(query, 60) FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;
toolkit.when: "the database is busy" with no obvious culprit

toolkit.what: Runs the query and shows the real plan with row counts, times and pages read.
flags: actually execute it (careful with writes: wrap them in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK)
pages hit in cache and read from disk
toolkit.example: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

toolkit.what: On the primary: one row per replica with its state and how far behind it is (next lesson).
flags: time since the last WAL the replica has applied
toolkit.example: SELECT application_name, state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;

toolkit.what: PgBouncer's admin console. `cl_waiting` above zero means clients are queueing for a server connection.
flags: clients with / waiting for a server connection
seconds the oldest waiting client has waited

steps.prompt: Configure PgBouncer to accept up to 5,000 client connections and return server connections after every transaction.
steps.explain: `max_client_conn` is how many apps may connect to PgBouncer; `default_pool_size` is how many real connections it opens per database and user pair. The second number is the one PostgreSQL feels.

steps.prompt: Match each observation to what it means.
pairs: Hundreds of rows in `pg_stat_activity` with state `idle`
Pools hold open connections that nobody is using right now
A client opened a transaction and stopped; it holds locks and a connection
Queries are queued behind a lock held by another transaction
Clients are waiting for a free server connection
steps.explain: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` so a stuck transaction is killed instead of blocking everyone behind its locks.

steps.title: Size the pools
prompt: - `int PoolSize(double queriesPerSec, double queryMs, double headroom)`: Little's law,
`queriesPerSec × queryMs / 1000`, times `1 + headroom`, rounded **up**, and never below `1`.
- `bool Fits(int instances, int pool, int maxConnections, int reserved)`: do `instances × pool` connections
- `int MaxPoolPerInstance(int instances, int maxConnections, int reserved)`: the largest pool each instance
may have so that they fit (whole connections). Throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when `instances <= 0`.
`PoolSize(400, 5, 0.5)` is `3`. 60 instances under `max_connections = 800` with 10 reserved may have
starter: int PoolSize(double queriesPerSec, double queryMs, double headroom) => 0;
bool Fits(int instances, int pool, int maxConnections, int reserved) => false;
int MaxPoolPerInstance(int instances, int maxConnections, int reserved) => 0;
solution: int PoolSize(double queriesPerSec, double queryMs, double headroom) =>
bool Fits(int instances, int pool, int maxConnections, int reserved) =>
int MaxPoolPerInstance(int instances, int maxConnections, int reserved)
hints: Busy connections = queries per second × seconds per query. Remember `queryMs / 1000`.
Integer division rounds down, which is what you want for the largest pool that still fits.
template: Dojo.Eq("400 q/s at 5 ms with 50 % headroom", 3, PoolSize(400, 5, 0.5));
Dojo.Eq("1,000 q/s at 12 ms with 25 % headroom", 15, PoolSize(1000, 12, 0.25));
Dojo.Check("60 × 20 does not fit in 800", !Fits(60, 20, 800, 10), "1,200 connections cannot fit in 790 slots");
Dojo.Check("60 × 13 fits in 790", Fits(60, 13, 800, 10), "780 connections fit in 790 slots");
steps.explain: Do this arithmetic for the **maximum** the autoscaler can reach, not today's instance count, and include every service and cron job that shares the database.

steps.title: Build it: too many connections
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *Too many connections*. The app tier was scaled out and now a share of
requests fail with "sorry, too many clients already" while the database CPU is calm. Make the connections
fit (a pooler in front of the database, or smaller pools) and get the error rate under the goal.
steps.explain: The board counts connections as instances × pool size against the database's limit, exactly the arithmetic from this lesson.
